title: The Internationale
artist: Eugène Pottier, music by Pierre De Geyter
note: Written by a Communard in hiding after the Paris Commune fell, and set to music in Lille 17 years later. It has been sung in almost every language since.

title: The Red Flag
note: Written on a London train after a dockers’ strike meeting, it became the anthem of the British Labour Party.

title: Solidarity Forever
note: Written for the IWW to the tune of “John Brown’s Body,” it is still sung at union meetings across North America.

title: There Is Power in a Union
note: One of Joe Hill’s songs for the IWW’s Little Red Songbook, written to the tune of a gospel hymn.
search: There Is Power in a Union Joe Hill

title: The Preacher and the Slave
note: Joe Hill’s parody of a Salvation Army hymn gave English the phrase “pie in the sky.”
search: The Preacher and the Slave Joe Hill

title: Joe Hill
note: A ballad in which the executed organizer appears in a dream, sung famously by Paul Robeson and by Joan Baez at Woodstock.

title: Which Side Are You On?
note: Written on a calendar page by a coal miner’s wife in Harlan County, Kentucky, after company men raided her home.
search: Which Side Are You On Florence Reece

title: Bread and Roses
artist: James Oppenheim, music by Mimi Fariña
note: A poem tied to the 1912 Lawrence textile strike, set to music by Mimi Fariña in 1974 and sung by Judy Collins.

title: Union Maid
note: Written after Guthrie and Pete Seeger visited striking workers in Oklahoma City.

title: This Land Is Your Land
note: Written as an angry answer to “God Bless America.” Some of its verses about private property and relief lines are often left out.
search: This Land Is Your Land Woody Guthrie

title: Ludlow Massacre
note: Guthrie’s ballad of the 1914 attack on the striking miners’ tent colony in southern Colorado.

title: 1913 Massacre
note: About the Italian Hall disaster in Calumet, Michigan, where 73 people, most of them children of striking copper miners, died in a stampede after a false fire alarm.

title: Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos)
artist: Woody Guthrie, music by Martin Hoffman
note: Guthrie wrote it after newspapers named the American crew of a crashed plane but called the Mexican farmworkers aboard only “deportees.”
search: Deportee Plane Wreck at Los Gatos

title: Talking Union
note: Pete Seeger and friends’ talking blues on how to organize a union, step by step.

title: Sixteen Tons
note: A coal miner’s lament about owing his soul to the company store, made a hit by Tennessee Ernie Ford in 1955.

title: Strange Fruit
note: Abel Meeropol, a Jewish communist schoolteacher in the Bronx, wrote this song about lynching. Holiday’s label refused to record it, so she went to another.

title: We Shall Overcome
artist: Traditional, adapted by the civil rights movement
note: Striking Black tobacco workers in Charleston sang an early version on their picket line in 1945. It passed through the Highlander Folk School to the civil rights movement.

title: Mississippi Goddam
note: Simone wrote it in about an hour after the murder of Medgar Evers and the bombing of the Birmingham church that killed four girls.

title: A Change Is Gonna Come
note: Cooke wrote it after being turned away from a whites-only motel in Louisiana, inspired by hearing Dylan’s “Blowin’ in the Wind.”
search: A Change Is Gonna Come Sam Cooke

title: Masters of War
note: Dylan’s furious address to the arms makers of the Cold War.

title: I Ain’t Marching Anymore
note: Ochs’s anti-war anthem, sung from the point of view of a soldier who has fought every American war.
search: I Aint Marching Anymore Phil Ochs

title: Ohio
note: Neil Young wrote it after seeing photographs of the Kent State shootings. It was recorded and released within weeks.

title: What’s Going On
note: Motown’s Berry Gordy didn’t want to release it, calling it too political. It went to number two and became the title track of a landmark album.

title: The Revolution Will Not Be Televised
note: A spoken-word poem over congas and flute that has been quoted at protests ever since.
search: The Revolution Will Not Be Televised Gil Scott-Heron

title: Get Up, Stand Up
note: Written after Marley toured Haiti and saw its poverty, it became the anthem of Amnesty International’s concerts.
search: Get Up Stand Up Bob Marley

title: Zombie
note: Fela mocked Nigerian soldiers as mindless zombies. In 1977 about a thousand soldiers attacked his compound, and his mother died of her injuries.

title: Bella Ciao
note: A song of the antifascist resistance whose melody may go back to the songs of women rice weeders in the Po valley.

title: A las barricadas
note: The anarchist anthem of the Spanish Civil War, set to the tune of the Polish revolutionary song “Warszawianka.”

title: Bandiera Rossa
note: “The red flag will triumph”: a song of Italian socialists, later sung by communists and partisans.

title: Grândola, Vila Morena
note: Played on Portuguese radio just after midnight on 25 April 1974 as the signal for the Carnation Revolution to begin.

title: Te recuerdo Amanda
note: A love song about factory workers Amanda and Manuel. Jara was killed in the days after the 1973 coup in Chile.

title: Plegaria a un labrador
note: A prayer addressed to a farm laborer, urging him to rise up together with his brothers.
search: Plegaria a un labrador Victor Jara

title: El pueblo unido jamás será vencido
note: Recorded in Chile months before the coup, its title became a chant at protests across the world.
search: El pueblo unido jamas sera vencido Quilapayun

title: Venceremos
note: The anthem of Salvador Allende’s Popular Unity campaign.

title: Hasta Siempre, Comandante
note: Puebla’s farewell to Che Guevara, written when Che left Cuba to fight abroad.

title: Nkosi Sikelel’ iAfrika
note: A Methodist hymn that became the anthem of the African National Congress and, in part, of democratic South Africa.

title: Biko
note: Gabriel’s lament for Steve Biko, who died from injuries sustained in South African police custody.

title: Free Nelson Mandela
note: A ska single that helped turn Mandela’s release into a cause across Britain.

title: Fight the Power
note: Commissioned by Spike Lee for Do the Right Thing, it plays throughout the film.

title: Alright
note: Its chorus became a chant at Black Lives Matter protests within months of release.

title: Step by Step
artist: Traditional, words from a miners’ union constitution
note: Its lyrics come from the preamble to the constitution of the American Miners’ Association: step by step the longest march can be won.

title: We Shall Not Be Moved
note: A spiritual turned into a union song by southern textile workers and miners, and later sung in the civil rights movement.

title: Ella’s Song
note: Bernice Johnson Reagon set the words of organizer Ella Baker to music: we who believe in freedom cannot rest.
search: Ellas Song Sweet Honey in the Rock
